items_missed: No agenda opener at the top of the call and no 'sound good?' confirmation. The closest thing came after the probe was already done — 'Okay, I'll start with the basic pricing and then we'll break down the quote for you. No need to take notes.' — which is a good mid-call roadmap but sets no timeframe and never asks the customer to agree to it.

No Worries Damage Coverage never pitched. Amy said only 'This also includes the taxes insurance and the gas' — the word 'insurance' with no explanation of the $2,000-per-move repair/replace/reimburse coverage, on a job with a king bed, a couch, a love seat and a dining table going down three flights with no elevator.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — notable because the customer specifically asked 'what would be the arrival times that you have available?' and Amy answered with windows ('morning we will arrive around 8:30 to nine', 'a two hour window') without ever attaching the guarantee that backs those windows.
'Pricing is super simple' framing not used — she went with 'let's start with basic' instead of the scripted opener.

Clock start never explained. The 2.5-hour minimum and 15-minute proration were both covered, but she never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens — and she leaned on prior-customer memory to carry it ('If you remember, we have a two and a half hour minimum') rather than restating the rule.

Save Your Ass was one line, not the prep speech. 'If you're able to take a car load or you know, disassemble the bed in advance that would help you save time and money by the end of the day' hits the carload tip and the time-equals-money logic, but there were zero consolidation examples (loose items in drawers, photos off walls, kids' toys, garden tools) and no 'does that make sense?' close — the customer redirected to mattress wrapping and the prep speech never resumed.

Box count never captured. The customer said 'maybe some boxes, like some box boxes' and Amy just echoed it back — 'But we just like another, some boxes. Okay. Some boxes.' — and moved on. On an hourly job with a storage stop, an unknown box count is a direct estimate-accuracy risk.
Special considerations never asked — no question about long walks, narrow hallways or tight turns, on a third-floor walk-up with a king bed and a couch.

Parking/access at the storage facility never asked. She got the address (1620 South I-35, Austin 78704) and the floor question, but not truck access, gate hours, or loading-dock/parking constraints at a facility on the I-35 frontage road.

Storage unit size left unresolved and dropped. Amy asked the right question — 'for reference one affect the estimate do you have a 5x5 5x10?' — the customer said 'I don't know it's not mine,' and she closed it with 'Yeah, no problem.' The single biggest unknown in the estimate was abandoned instead of routed to a follow-up ('can you text me the unit number and I'll size it from there').

No booking attempt on the call. Amy never asked for the business — no 'we have Monday open, want me to lock that in for you right now?' When the customer said 'let me think about this and I will give you a callback,' she accepted it and put the action on him: 'just give us a call as soon as possible. So we can lock the date for you.' A returning customer with a confirmed date three days out, a quote he called back about, and no deposit required went unbooked.

Email handoff mentioned but not structured — no BOLDED-details-at-the-top framing and no 'reply with any corrections,' even though the whole point of the promised email was that the numbers had changed from the original apartment-to-apartment quote.
Hours and how to reach us never given. 'Just give us a call as soon as possible' with no phone number, no hours, and no named callback path.

Walk distance, equivalents (school-bus reference) and traffic never used as estimate variables — the storage stop is on I-35 on a Monday morning and drive/traffic time was never named as a factor in the 4-to-5-hour budget.

No Ecobox or Sparefoot referral despite two open doors: the customer has a storage unit he doesn't own the details of, and said of a spare couch 'which I have not figured out what to do with that yet.'

Customer's name used twice and mangled both times — 'Oh, yeah, maxim not connect me if I got it right?' and the farewell 'Thank you Maxine you have a good day.' He had already introduced himself simply: 'my name is Max.' Short of the 3+ standard, and the sign-off used the wrong name.
top_strength: The pricing mechanics and the estimate math were genuinely good, and the returning-customer recognition was the best moment on the call. Amy pulled the history unprompted and used it: 'It looks like you moved with us, I was able to pull up an old profile under your name. We moved with us in 2023 we moved you into this apartment actually. Would you say you have the same inventory or more?' — that is a fast, accurate inventory shortcut and it made the customer feel known. She opened by confirming the details on file rather than re-interviewing him ('you're moving out of a one bedroom apartment. Third floor no elevator... 12220 hunters chase drive and we are moving you to a second floor apartment with elevator this time. In 1000 San Marco Street'), and she flagged the quote change honestly before quoting: 'the first one I sent earlier is just for the apartment to apartment... but with this additional stop, additional time, of course.' The all-inclusive rundown was complete and correct — '$208 per hour with two movers... moving blankets, shrink [wrap] bands Dolly, the tools or any disassemble or reassembly that needs to be done. This also includes the taxes insurance and the gas' — with the trip fee isolated cleanly ('the only thing outside of the hourly rate is what we call a travel fee amounting to $75') and the no-hidden-fees points landed ('no credit card fees, no terrible disassemble assembly fees'). Her estimate was well-reasoned and the arithmetic checks out: 'two movers, one truck, two and a half to three and a half hours with the additional stop. And then the, you know, third floor [stairs] involved, I would suggest budget for four maybe, up to five hours just to be a bit conservative' — $907 at four hours and $1,115 at five, both correct at $208/hr plus the $75 fee. She also volunteered the day-of-week tiers without being pushed ('Monday to Thursday is the cheapest same pricing, $208' vs '$210 per hour on Sunday') and framed it in the customer's favor: 'you're not [bound] by the estimate. Basically just pay for the actual time.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: ask for the booking. This was the warmest possible setup — a repeat Einstein customer who called back on a voicemail, whose date was already Monday September 7th, who got a clean quote he didn't argue with, and who needs no deposit — and Amy never once asked him to book. When he said 'let me think about this and I will give you a callback,' the line she needed was: 'Max, Monday morning at 8:30 is open right now and there's no deposit to hold it — let me lock that in for you and you can call me back to cancel or change anything up until Sunday. That way you're not gambling on the last slot three days out.' She had the urgency argument and used it in the weakest possible direction, telling him to call her. Second priority: pair the differentiators to the anxiety points he handed her. He asked about arrival windows — that is the On-Time Guarantee cue: 'We'll be there between 8:30 and 9, and if we miss that window we start discounting your bill immediately.' He worried out loud about his mattress ('well, we have like a mattress wrapper') — that is the No Worries cue: 'We shrink-wrap it and blanket it, and on top of that our No Worries Damage Coverage covers up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse any accidental damage, so you're not carrying that risk.' And Meet Your Mover should have closed the call: 'A few days before Monday you'll get an email with a photo and a quick intro to the mover coming to your door.' Three differentiators, three open invitations, zero taken. Third: the Save Your Ass speech got one sentence and then evaporated. Rebuild it as a block — carload, loose items out of drawers, photos off walls, kids' and closet items boxed, then 'does that make sense?' — because on a third-floor walk-up this is the section that actually protects the estimate. Estimate-accuracy risks to close in EMMA today: (1) the storage unit size is unknown and the customer doesn't own the unit — get him to text the unit number or a photo before Monday, because 'one bed, one desk, one couch, maybe some boxes' from an unsized unit is exactly the input that produces a 4-hour quote and a 6-hour actual; (2) box count is unquantified at both origin and storage; (3) she quoted 4-5 hours conservatively, which is the right instinct, but the conservatism is covering a data gap rather than a known job — note in EMMA that the range is wide because the storage contents are unverified, so the accuracy miss isn't scored against the rep later.
phone_presence_notes: Real warmth and good energy throughout — 'It was me who left you a voicemail earlier. Thank you so much for calling us back. How are you doing today?', 'Doing well, thank you so much for asking', plus 'Amazing', 'Gotcha!' and 'Nice' as natural acknowledgments — undercut only by getting his name wrong twice, including in the farewell ('Thank you Maxine').
audio_review_reason: Amy's side of the transcript is heavily garbled in the pricing stretch ('$208.208 per hour', 'shrink crap bands', 'no terrible fees', 'third floor Stas involved', 'a two hour window between twelve to morning', 'Ar then', 'Sor'), and the customer misheard the Sunday rate as '$2,100' when she said $210 — so clarity and pace during the money portion cannot be judged from text alone and the score of 4 may be generous on delivery.
